title: Apparent Alternatives, Shared Bottlenecks: A Structural Redundancy Audit of a Real European Freight Corridor
content: Freight corridors are widely assumed to be resilient when multiple route alternatives exist between key logistics nodes. However, route multiplicity—the existence of several candidate paths—does not guarantee structural redundancy in the graph-theoretic sense, where independent paths must not share critical intermediate nodes or edges [1,2]. Recent infrastructure disruptions in European logistics networks have exposed this assumption as operationally dangerous, motivating a rigorous structural analysis of apparent corridor alternatives [3,4]. A directed corridor graph was constructed from filtered road-network data covering the Benelux region and northern France. An expanded origin–destination audit was performed using nine anchor cities, generating 72 ordered OD pairs, or 71 after excluding one degenerate pair identified during data validation. For each pair, shortest paths, near-shortest alternatives, overlap metrics, bottleneck frequencies, and exact node connectivity were evaluated. Of the 71 corrected OD pairs, 28 were reachable and 27 exhibited at least two near-shortest alternatives. All retained candidate paths fell within 0.40% of the shortest-path cost, and the alternatives overlapped heavily, repeatedly traversing the same nodes and edges. Despite this multiplicity, exact connectivity validation across all 28 reachable pairs showed node connectivity equal to one for 27 of them, confirming dependence on single structural bottlenecks. The sole exception, Antwerp–Lille (k = 2), proved on closer inspection to be geographically fragile in its own right: its two formally independent paths converge within 60 metres of each other at the Lille motorway gateway. These findings have direct implications for infrastructure resilience auditing: route counting alone is insufficient to assess corridor robustness, and targeted structural investment in identified bottleneck locations is required to achieve meaningful redundancy.
